front: In Hudson's view, what are two ways the body stops an emotion?
back: Raising the chin, and clamping the jaw.
extra: He says lowering the chin tends to let you feel more. He links the raised chin to people who cannot feel their emotions.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: Try now, 1 minute: recall a mild feeling. Lift your chin, then lower it. What do you notice?
back: Notice whether the feeling gets stronger when the chin is down.
extra: In the session, Ali Abdaal felt it more strongly with his chin lowered.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: What goal does Hudson offer in place of the usual career goals (a book, an income, more views)?
back: Be 10% more connected in everything I do.
extra: Connected to yourself and to others. Nothing practical has to change. This is different from keeping 10% of your attention in your body.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: What two questions does Hudson put to a dull, routine work task?
back: How could the whole team do this in the most connected way? And can I think about it while I am connected with myself?
extra: With sponsor segments, Ali Abdaal at once had new ideas, such as working with brands he actually uses. Hudson says the same question works for anything, even buying equipment.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: When you feel a new insight, why does Hudson say not to write it down at once?
back: Writing it down at once can stop it from settling in the body. Let it land first, then write.
extra: He says what resonates in the body is often remembered better than a list you may never read again.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: What does Hudson mean by "emotional abuse"?
back: Someone held you responsible for their emotional state, or told you your emotions were not okay to have.
extra: His examples: "Don't be so excited", "Don't cry". He says he uses the word loosely, by his own definition.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: Hudson asks two things of someone who says they cannot feel. What is the distinction?
back: How much is not feeling, and how much is not being aware that you feel?
extra: Ali Abdaal's brother would see tears in his eyes before Ali knew anything was happening. The body was feeling; the awareness lagged.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: Hudson's story: how did he first learn that he was afraid, before he could feel fear in his body?
back: He noticed his thinking had gone black or white, and took that as a sign of fear.
extra: Only later did he learn what fear felt like in his body. His body was in fear either way.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: Try now, 3 minutes: call up a memory of love, then one of sorrow. Go back and forth a few times. Then hold both at once. What do you notice?
back: Notice where each one sits in your body, and what the love does to the space around the sorrow.
extra: For Ali Abdaal, sorrow was a squeeze under his ribs. Love eased it and brought a sense of space.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: When the facts say you will be fine, how does Hudson suggest you keep them without burying the sadness?
back: Let both be there: "That's all true, but I'm sad."
extra: Ali Abdaal talked himself out of a heartbreak with counter-examples, and Hudson says he chose success over connection then.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: Hudson says you do not need a meaning to have an emotion. What is his evidence?
back: Mammals with little or no thought still have emotions.
extra: He agrees that the meaning you make can create emotions. He says it is not the only route.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

text: Hudson says no single emotion lasts more than {{c1::a second}}, but you are never awake without {{c2::some emotion}}, like music that is always playing in the background.
extra: Ali Abdaal had read that an emotion lasts about 45 seconds unless a story feeds it. Hudson put it this way instead: sadness comes back thousands of times, each with a different seasoning.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: Hudson's story: what happened to his feeling "I can't get my dad's love" after he moved away?
back: It became "I can't get money": the same longing with a new story.
extra: His point: an emotional rut can swap its story to keep itself going. Every story has some falsehood in it, and believing one can stall the emotion.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: Ali Abdaal works to "get to a place of okayness". What does Hudson point out?
back: That plan means you have to be not okay to get to okay.
extra: If you were okay already, the reason to work would be connection and fun, not lack.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: What question did Hudson ask Ali Abdaal about his bestseller win?
back: What would it look like to celebrate it in the most connected way?
extra: Ali saw thank-you gifts and a month of rest, and felt gratitude. Hudson asked if, after two years, he would be ahead or behind. Ali said ahead. Hudson: that is how much emotions matter to productivity.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)
key: What question did Hudson ask about Ali Abdaal's bestseller win, and what came of it?

front: In a coaching session, what does Hudson say the client's very first remark usually holds?
back: The kernel of what the session will work on.
extra: He says he follows the client rather than leading them.
source_title: How Connection Can Change Your Life (Joe Hudson & Ali Abdaal)

front: The four-year list, step 1: what do you write?
back: Everything you have tried to change about yourself for at least four years.
extra: Examples: how you eat, who you spend time with, speaking your mind. Do step 1 before you read step 2.
source_title: Why You Can't Change

front: The four-year list, step 2: what do you tick?
back: Each item you feel obligation or shame about, as if something is wrong with you unless it changes.
extra: Notice how many of the long-stuck items carry that shame. He says this shows how badly shame works as a tool for change.
source_title: Why You Can't Change

front: Hudson's story at about 28: what did he find when he reread his list of hard truths about himself?
back: Every item that had not changed was one he told himself he "should" change.
extra: He had written the list, folded it away, and found it six to eight months later.
source_title: Why You Can't Change

text: The "should" cycle: you tell yourself you should, you {{c1::don't do it}}, you {{c2::beat yourself up}}, and you tell yourself you should again.
extra: He says the word "should" alone makes the body contract.
source_title: Why You Can't Change

text: Hudson quotes a spiritual teacher: shame is the {{c1::lock}} that keeps the chains of bad habits in place.
extra: He says shame holds back other emotions, so you never feel them all the way through, and the pattern repeats.
source_title: Why You Can't Change

front: What does Hudson call the first step to drop shame?
back: Notice each place you shame yourself, and see how gentle you can be in that moment.
extra: Then use Emotional Inquiry to feel the emotions the shame held back.
source_title: Why You Can't Change

front: Hudson's story: what were the last words of his friend's dying mother?
back: That she had felt all her life that something was wrong with her, and what a waste that was.
extra: He calls her words the clue to a life without regret.
source_title: Be yourself and watch your life rearrange | Part 1

front: In Hudson's view, what does regret after a conversation usually mean?
back: You wanted an outcome and did not get it, or are not sure you got it.
extra: Since you will never always get the result, outcome-based action always brings some regret.
source_title: Be yourself and watch your life rearrange | Part 1

front: How could you act so that you would have no regret even if the result were the same?
back: Be 100% true to yourself, so you are proud of how you behaved before you know the result.
extra: He calls this being self-possessed.
source_title: Be yourself and watch your life rearrange | Part 1

front: Why does contorting yourself to get a result not pay off, in Hudson's view?
back: Whatever says yes is saying yes to the contorted version. Being yourself draws people who like you for you.
extra: He says you design a life by being yourself: the people who pay you, like you and believe in you do so for who you are.
source_title: Be yourself and watch your life rearrange | Part 1

text: Regret a conversation and you will likely regret the {{c1::day}}; regret the day and you will likely regret the {{c2::year}}, then your {{c3::life}}.
extra: So the simple rule, he says, is to act in a way that makes you proud.
source_title: Be yourself and watch your life rearrange | Part 1

front: The seven-day regret experiment: what do you do each day?
back: Take one regret. Ask how you could have acted to feel no regret, whatever the outcome. Then act that way in the next worrying situation.
extra: Each day is one iteration. At the end of the week, notice how much regret you feel. The fears that stop you are the things you will regret.
source_title: Be yourself and watch your life rearrange | Part 1

front: Try now, 1 minute: breathe once and ask yourself a question about right now. What is the question?
back: What is required in this moment to be good with myself?
extra: If the answer runs into the future or the past, bring it back to now.
source_title: Why Self-Possessed People Get Everything They Want

front: In Hudson's view, what are you often really after when you chase approval or avoid judgment?
back: The feeling of being good with yourself, which is always available now.
extra: Approval never delivers it: someone who does not judge you today judges you tomorrow.
source_title: Why Self-Possessed People Get Everything They Want

front: What does Hudson say you will certainly meet if you leave the house today?
back: Someone's disappointment, judgment or criticism.
extra: Trying to keep everyone happy with you separates you from yourself.
source_title: Why Self-Possessed People Get Everything They Want

front: In business and families, Hudson often sees one person chasing and one running. What is the alternative?
back: Two people standing upright in themselves.
extra: The upright one thinks: people will judge me or like me, I will mess up, and I still have me.
source_title: Why Self-Possessed People Get Everything They Want

front: In Hudson's view, what does it mean when someone judges or criticises you?
back: They feel unseen, in themselves or by others.
extra: So ask: "What do you mean? What am I missing? What would you have me do?" They do not need you to agree, only to feel heard.
source_title: Why Self-Possessed People Get Everything They Want

front: Hudson's college story: who did people at the bar want?
back: The self-possessed ones, men and women alike. The needy, chasing ones rarely got what they really wanted.
source_title: Why Self-Possessed People Get Everything They Want

front: Why does winning feel so good, in an idea Hudson credits (he thinks) to Eckhart Tolle?
back: For a minute or a day, you are not thinking about what you have to do next.
extra: A champion golfer said the feeling of winning lasts only a few minutes before the next question comes.
source_title: I've Coached 100s of Top Performers. This is the Moment I Look For

front: Some say "everything comes and goes" is a sad view. What does Hudson draw from it?
back: Freedom: since there will always be a next win and a next failure, you are free to enjoy.
source_title: I've Coached 100s of Top Performers. This is the Moment I Look For

front: Why are the kings, not the holy men, the ones who become enlightened in the scriptures, as Hudson tells it from a friend?
back: Kings get everything they thought would fulfil them and find the hole is still not filled.
extra: He says he knows many who reached their dreams, some with $100 million, who still felt it was not what they needed.
source_title: I've Coached 100s of Top Performers. This is the Moment I Look For

front: Where does Hudson say the real transformational journey begins?
back: When you see nothing external will make you whole, and turn to explore the empty space you tried to fill.
extra: Ask what is there, and how to stop avoiding it. He says the thing you avoided can be the most direct path to freedom.
source_title: I've Coached 100s of Top Performers. This is the Moment I Look For

front: Try now, 1 minute: say aloud "I want [someone I love] to be happy", then "I want [a large sum of money]". What do you compare?
back: How your body responds to each: tightening, speeding up, or ease and love.
extra: He then asks: what is it okay for you to want, and what not? He means emotionally, not logically.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: Why did Hudson ask a client why he said "abundance" instead of "I want to be filthy rich"?
back: He says the word "abundance" often signals guilt over having money.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: What image did Hudson use to show the client his belief that he must add value to deserve love?
back: A parent looking at a newborn and saying "I won't love you until you add value".
extra: The client felt it as a dagger. Hudson says a child raised that way becomes needy, and neediness drives clients away.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: What habit did Hudson catch three times in one session, and what does it do?
back: Turning each insight into a task to do so you can earn love. It destroys the insight.
extra: "Just be who I am fully" became an almost impossible task; Hudson asked if he deserved love at half, or 10%.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: Hudson's view: what can heavy positive thinking ("you can do it!") hide?
back: Doubt. You would never tell Bill Gates he can make $200.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: How does Hudson show that you are not fully responsible for your results?
back: Trace them back: results come from time, time from priorities, priorities from thoughts, and you cannot choose your next thought.
extra: He says the sense of total responsibility had made the client stuck for five years, not productive.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: Try now, 1 minute: imagine you are not responsible for any of it, and neither is anyone else. What do you notice?
back: Notice any lightness or relief, and whether you would really do nothing.
extra: Hudson asks: at seven, did you do nothing? Play and curiosity got things done without the burden.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: Hudson asks if any choice in life will ever be free of consequences. What does the answer show?
back: No. So an idea of freedom that needs no consequences is one more hurdle you set yourself.
extra: Technically you are always free to choose; there are always consequences.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: Why does Hudson say the fear of losing a good feeling makes no sense?
back: All states come and go. You finish an ice cream, but you are not scared of ice cream.
extra: A great meal eaten every day would soon stop being great. Passing is what makes it sweet.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: Try now: without going into the past or the future, ask "What is wrong with me right now?" What then?
back: If nothing is wrong right now, ask what the task list is for and what you are trying to earn.
extra: He warns that even trying to keep the good feeling becomes a new task.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

front: What does Hudson say is more effective than telling yourself you have to be a certain way?
back: Getting in touch with what is true right now.
extra: "I need to be present" is not true: you are always present. True now: you are free, you have enough, and you need not earn love.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)

text: Accepting an emotion so it will leave is like letting your {{c1::son}} into the house only because you want him to grow up and move out.
extra: Hudson's image for why welcoming must be real, not a way to get better. He says self-help tools stop working once you use them to fix yourself: they turn into criticism.
source_title: Why you keep sabotaging your own success (Coaching with Joe)
